title: Superlinear cell-probe lower bounds for succinct Boolean matrix-vector products
formal:
For every family of deterministic exact static cell-probe data structures representing arbitrary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) in \(n^2+o(n^2)\) bits, with word length
\[w_n=\left\lceil\log_2(n^2+1)\right\rceil,\]
must its worst-case number \(T(n)\) of word probes for answering a Boolean matrix-vector query satisfy
\[T(n)=\omega(n)?\]
The representation may encode the whole matrix arbitrarily; it need not retain the original matrix as a separately readable array. Computation between probes and preprocessing time are uncharged, as specified below.
why: A superlinear lower bound with almost no storage overhead would go beyond the standard static-data-structure barriers for this central problem. It would isolate an information-access obstruction independently of how much computation is performed between memory reads.
status_note: Source-open for the explicitly stated general succinct deterministic cell-probe model. The complete 2017 problem page and the original upper-bound theorem were checked; the 2018 paper’s main results explicitly concern systematic representations, with the stated lower theorem counting original matrix entries. Its unrestricted-redundancy word-probe conversion and representation restriction do not establish this exact target. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution. This is a source/formulation and theorem-scope review, not independent verification or Lean formalization of every cited proof.

importance.reason: A fundamental unconditional lower-bound target for a central matrix-query problem. Its importance lies in handling general succinct encodings and adaptive word probes, beyond strong but representation-specific known results.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary Boolean matrix, stored using only a vanishing fraction of extra bits beyond its n²-bit information content.
A query asks for the entire Boolean product with one vector, charging only logarithmic-word memory probes.
The target asks whether every deterministic exact adaptive structure needs a worst-case probe count growing faster than n.
Known strong tradeoffs retain the original matrix layout and count individual entries, so their scope and word-size conversion matter.
The card keeps arbitrary succinct encodings and all subquadratic redundancies rather than substituting a narrower solved model.

definitions:
For \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and a query \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\), the required answer is the entire vector \(y=Mv\in\{0,1\}^n\) over the Boolean semiring:
\[y_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^n(M_{ij}\wedge v_j),\qquad i\in[n].\]
Here \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) are logical AND and OR. This is not multiplication over the two-element field, where addition would instead be parity. Every matrix and every query vector is allowed.

For each integer \(n\ge2\), choose an integer number of memory cells \(S_n\), with \(1\le S_n\le2^{w_n}\), and an encoding map
\[E_n:\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\longrightarrow(\{0,1\}^{w_n})^{S_n}.\]
The stored memory on input \(M\) is exactly \(E_n(M)\). All persistent matrix-dependent information must be in these cells. The space bound includes padding to complete words: define \(r_n=S_nw_n-n^2\), and require \(r_n\ge0\) and \(r_n/n^2\to0\). This is the meaning of succinct storage. No particular rate such as \(r_n=n^{7/4}\), and no smaller fixed redundancy budget, is imposed.

The query gets \(n\) and \(v\) for free, plus access to the stored cells at addresses \(0,\ldots,S_n-1\). One probe reads one entire \(w_n\)-bit word. The next address may depend on the query and all words previously read. Arbitrary finite computation and temporary workspace between probes cost nothing; reading the query vector and producing the output vector also cost nothing. Temporary state starts empty apart from the query and public size parameters, so there is no free matrix-dependent advice. The representation is static and read-only, and each query starts afresh; no state left by earlier queries is available.

Equivalently, for each \(n\) and query \(v\), the query rule is a finite decision tree whose internal nodes specify cell addresses, whose outgoing edges are indexed by possible word contents, and whose leaves specify an output vector. Its leaves must give the correct \(Mv\) on every stored encoding. The trees and their computations may depend on \(n\) and \(v\), but not on \(M\) except through the probed words. There is no restriction on their description size or on the encoding's preprocessing time. Thus the lower bound is in the usual permissive, nonuniform cell-probe model; restricting the query computation to an efficient word-RAM program would be a different target. The formulation fixes the deterministic exact version: no random coins or error probability are allowed in the data structures quantified over here.

For one such family \(\mathcal D\), let
\[T_{\mathcal D}(n)=\max_{M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n},\ v\in\{0,1\}^n}
\#\{\text{word probes on query }v\text{ after storing }M\}.\]
Repeated reads count repeatedly. The assertion means that for every eligible family \(\mathcal D\) and every real \(C>0\), some \(n_0\) satisfies \(T_{\mathcal D}(n)>Cn\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The threshold may depend on the family and \(C\). The fixed choice \(w_n=\Theta(\log n)\) makes words large enough for cell addresses without allowing one word to hold the whole matrix.

A systematic representation stores the unchanged matrix and separate redundant bits. That is a restriction on \(E_n\), not part of this general succinct target. The source page does not require that restriction; its example upper bound happens to have it. The distinction matters for applying later lower bounds.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal superlinear lower bound. An affirmative answer must cover every deterministic exact representation and adaptive query family with the stated \(n^2+o(n^2)\) total storage. A negative answer must exhibit an eligible family, a constant \(C>0\), and arbitrarily large \(n\) with \(T(n)\le Cn\); a bound holding at all sufficiently large sizes is sufficient but not necessary to negate the displayed limit. A lower bound only for systematic encodings, nonadaptive queries, smaller redundancy, individual matrix-entry probes, or charged word-RAM computation does not establish this statement without the needed conversion. This is exact asymptotic yes/no acceptance, not an approximation of a finite running time.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether succinct data structures for Boolean matrix-vector multiplication must use more than a linear number of cell probes per query.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Problem 75; general succinct encoding, exact deterministic queries and logarithmic word size are made explicit

context_blocks.text: The matrix contains n² independent bits, but one query asks only for n Boolean answers. Preprocessing can reorganize the information before any query arrives. The question asks whether nearly minimal storage still forces substantially more than n memory accesses on a worst-case query, even when all arithmetic and logical work is free.

The source contrasts this model with the online matrix-vector conjecture for ordinary computation. A time lower bound in a word-RAM model charges operations that the cell-probe model ignores. The online conjecture therefore cannot simply be substituted for an unconditional memory-access lower bound.

Larsen and Williams give a deterministic cell-probe structure using \(O(n^{7/4}/\sqrt w)\) probes per query and only \(O(n^{7/4}\sqrt w)\) bits beyond the stored matrix. With logarithmic words this is succinct and polynomially faster in probe count than scanning all matrix entries. It remains superlinear and hence does not refute the proposed lower bound.

The 2018 paper proves a much stronger tradeoff for systematic representations. Its Theorem 1.2 gives \(t_{\rm bit}r=\Omega(n^3)\) when \(n\le r\le n^2/4\), even for queries correct with probability at least \(1-1/n\), and permits reading all redundant bits. Here \(t_{\rm bit}\) counts original matrix entries, not words. A word-probe consequence loses a factor of \(w\), yielding \(\Omega(n^3/(rw))\) in that restricted representation model.

Two qualifications prevent that theorem from settling this card as stated. It retains the matrix in its original layout, whereas a general succinct representation may encode every bit differently. Moreover, even its word-probe consequence is superlinear only for suitably smaller redundancy; arbitrary o(n²) redundancy need not be o(n²/w). The title of a succinct-data-structure theorem alone does not establish the general claim.

The same paper improves the systematic upper bound to roughly n³ᐟ² probes and redundant bits, up to logarithmic factors at logarithmic word size, using randomized queries. This is useful progress on the tradeoff, while the exact deterministic lower-bound question here remains a separately specified target.
